# arrayref - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arrayref/

## Expand description

This package contains just four macros, which enable the creation of array references to portions of arrays or slices (or things that can be sliced).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Here is a simple example of slicing and dicing a slice into array
references with these macros.  Here we implement a simple
little-endian conversion from bytes to `u16`, and demonstrate code
that uses `array_ref!` to extract an array reference from a larger
array.  Note that the documentation for each macro also has an
example of its use.

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate arrayref;
fn read_u16(bytes: &[u8; 2]) -> u16 {
     bytes[0] as u16 + ((bytes[1] as u16) << 8)
}
// ...
let data = [0,1,2,3,4,0,6,7,8,9];
assert_eq!(256, read_u16(array_ref![data,0,2]));
assert_eq!(4, read_u16(array_ref![data,4,2]));
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [array_](https://docs.rs/macro.array_mut_ref.html)- mut_ - ref
- You can use `array_mut_ref`to generate a mutable array reference to a subset of a sliceable bit of data (which could be an array, or a slice, or a Vec).
- [array_](https://docs.rs/macro.array_ref.html)- ref
- You can use `array_ref`to generate an array reference to a subset of a sliceable bit of data (which could be an array, or a slice, or a Vec).
- [array_](https://docs.rs/macro.array_refs.html)- refs
- You can use `array_refs`to generate a series of array references to an input array reference. The idea is if you want to break an array into a series of contiguous and non-overlapping arrays.`array_refs`is a bit funny in that it insists on slicing up the*entire*array. This is intentional, as I find it handy to make me ensure that my sub-arrays add up to the entire array. This macro will*never*panic, since the sizes are all checked at compile time.
- [mut_](https://docs.rs/macro.mut_array_refs.html)- array_ - refs
- You can use `mut_array_refs`to generate a series of mutable array references to an input mutable array reference. The idea is if you want to break an array into a series of contiguous and non-overlapping mutable array references. Like`array_refs!`,`mut_array_refs!`is a bit funny in that it insists on slicing up the*entire*array. This is intentional, as I find it handy to make me ensure that my sub-arrays add up to the entire array. This macro will*never*panic, since the sizes are all checked at compile time.

# arrayref - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arrayref/0.3.9/arrayref/

## Expand description

This package contains just four macros, which enable the creation of array references to portions of arrays or slices (or things that can be sliced).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Here is a simple example of slicing and dicing a slice into array

assert_eq!(4, read_u16(array_ref![data,4,2]));

# arrayref 0.3.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/arrayref/latest

# arrayref

This is a very small rust module, which contains just four macros, for the taking of array references to slices of... sliceable things. These macros (which are awkwardly named) should be perfectly safe, and have seen just a tad of code review.

## Why would I want this?

The goal of arrayref is to enable the effective use of APIs that
involve array references rather than slices, for situations where
parameters must have a given size.  As an example, consider the
`byteorder` crate.  This is a very nice crate with a simple API
containing functions that look like:

```
;
;
```
Looking at this, you might wonder why they accept a slice reference as input. After all, they always want just two bytes. These functions must panic if given a slice that is too small, which means that unless they are inlined, then a runtime bounds-check is forced, even if it may be statically known that the input is the right size.

Wouldn't it be nicer if we had functions more like

```
;
;
```
The type signature would tell users precisely what size of input is
required, and the compiler could check at compile time that the input
is of the appropriate size: this sounds like the zero-cost
abstractions rust is famous for!  However, there is a catch, which
arises when you try to *use* these nicer functions, which is that
usually you are looking at two bytes in a stream.  So, e.g. consider
that we are working with a hypothetical (and simplified) ipv6 address.

Doing this with our array version (which looks so beautiful in terms of accurately describing what we want!) looks terrible:

```
let addr: & = ...;
let mut segments = ;
// array-based API
for i in 0 .. 8
// slice-based API
for i in 0 .. 8
```
The array-based approach looks way worse.  We need to create a fresh
copy of the bytes, just so it will be in an array of the proper size!
Thus the whole "zero-cost abstraction" argument for using array
references fails.  The trouble is that there is no (safe) way (until
[RFC 495](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/0495-array-pattern-changes.md) lands) to obtain an array reference to a portion of a
larger array or slice.  Doing so is the equivalent of taking a slice
with a size known at compile time, and ought to be built into the
language.

The arrayref crate allows you to do this kind of slicing. So the above (very contrived) example can be implemented with array references as:

```
let addr: & = ...;
let mut segments = ;
// array-based API with arrayref
for i in 0 .. 8
```
Here the `array_ref![addr,2*i,2]` macro allows us to take an array
reference to a slice consisting of two bytes starting at `2*i`.  Apart
from the syntax (less nice than slicing), it is essentially the same
as the slice approach.  However, this code makes explicit the
need for precisely *two* bytes both in the caller, and in the function
signature.

This module provides three other macros providing related
functionality, which you can read about in the
[documentation](https://droundy.github.io/arrayref).

For an example of how these macros can be used in an actual program,
see [my rust translation of tweetnacl](https://github.com/droundy/onionsalt/blob/master/src/crypto/mod.rs), which uses `arrayref`
to almost exclusively accept array references in functions, with the
only exception being those which truly expect data of arbitrary
length.  In my opinion, the result is code that is far more legible
than the original C code, since the size of each argument is
explicit.  Moreover (although I have not tested this), the use of
array references rather than slices *should* result in far fewer
bounds checks, since almost all sizes are known at compile time.

---

# quickcheck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quickcheck/^1.0/

## Expand description

This crate is a port of
[Haskell’s QuickCheck](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/QuickCheck).

QuickCheck is a library for random testing of program properties. The programmer provides a specification of the program, in the form of properties which functions should satisfy, and QuickCheck then tests that the properties hold in a large number of randomly generated cases.

For detailed examples, please see the
[README](https://github.com/BurntSushi/quickcheck).

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

In general, this crate considers the `Arbitrary` implementations provided as
implementation details. Strategies may or may not change over time, which may
cause new test failures, presumably due to the discovery of new bugs due to a
new kind of witness being generated. These sorts of changes may happen in
semver compatible releases.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/macro.quickcheck.html)
- A macro for writing quickcheck tests.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Gen](https://docs.rs/struct.Gen.html)
- `Gen`represents a PRNG.
- [NoShrink](https://docs.rs/struct.NoShrink.html)
- Wrapper for disabling shrinking for an Arbitrary
- [Quick](https://docs.rs/struct.QuickCheck.html)- Check
- The main `QuickCheck`type for setting configuration and running`QuickCheck`.
- [Test](https://docs.rs/struct.TestResult.html)- Result
- Describes the status of a single instance of a test.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- `Arbitrary`describes types whose values can be randomly generated and shrunk.
- [Testable](https://docs.rs/trait.Testable.html)
- `Testable`describes types (e.g., a function) whose values can be tested.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [empty_](https://docs.rs/fn.empty_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with zero elements.
- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/fn.quickcheck.html)
- Convenience function for running `QuickCheck`.
- [single_](https://docs.rs/fn.single_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with a single element.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# Releases - Docs.rs

# surtgis_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/surtgis-core/0.17.0/surtgis_core/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#surtgis-core)SurtGis Core

Core types, traits and I/O for the SurtGis geospatial library.

This crate provides:

- `Raster<T>`: Generic raster grid type
- `GeoTransform`: Affine transformation for georeferencing
- `CRS`: Coordinate Reference System handling
- Algorithm traits for consistent API
- I/O for common geospatial formats
- Streaming (`StripProcessor``TileGrid`

[§](https://docs.rs#stability)Stability

As of v0.15.0, `surtgis-core` is the foundation of the SurtGIS
engine ecosystem and its public API is treated as **stable under
SemVer**: within a minor series the API only grows, and breaking
changes are pre-announced one release ahead in the CHANGELOG under
a `Breaking` heading. Sibling crates should depend on
`surtgis-core = "0.15"` alone; the CLI and GUI crates carry no
stability promise.

# kigumi_schema - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kigumi-schema/0.1.0/kigumi_schema/

## Expand description

The projections: from a `ResolvedModel` to Postgres DDL and an agnostic UI contract (JSON).

Same source of truth → multiple outputs. The UI contract carries visibility/readonly rules as
a portable [ Domain](https://docs.rs/kigumi-core/0.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/kigumi_core/domain/enum.Domain.html) JSON AST — the frontend evaluates them client-side from data, never an
eval’d string, and they are the SAME domains the server compiles to SQL.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldRule.html)- Rule
- A dynamic UI rule bound to a field: when `domain`holds for a record, the field becomes invisible/readonly. The domain is a thunk because a`Domain`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [openapi](https://docs.rs/fn.openapi.html)
- Builds a pretty-printed OpenAPI 3.1 document describing `models`.
- [pg_](https://docs.rs/fn.pg_add_column_type.html)- add_ - column_ - type
- The column TYPE plus its foreign-key reference for an additive `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN`— the subset of`to_ddl`’s column spec WITHOUT NOT NULL / UNIQUE / CHECK / DEFAULT, so it is safe to add to a populated table (the column is simply NULL on existing rows; required-ness is enforced at the write layer).`None`for kinds with no own column (One2many / Many2many).
- [pg_](https://docs.rs/fn.pg_column_type.html)- column_ - type
- Postgres SQL type for a field with a column.
The Postgres column type for a field kind — used by `to_ddl`and by the runtime custom-field`ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN`. Empty string for kinds that have no own column (One2many/Many2many).
- [to_ddl](https://docs.rs/fn.to_ddl.html)
- Generates the `CREATE TABLE`. Non-stored computed fields and one2many produce no columns.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_ui_contract.html)- ui_ - contract
- Agnostic UI contract: JSON consumable by ANY frontend. Computed fields are readonly; dynamic
`invisible_when`/`readonly_when`rules are emitted as portable domain ASTs.

# crabenv 0.0.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/crabenv/0.0.4

# 🦀 crabenv

The simplest, opinionated way to keep .env files, schemas, and examples aligned.

`crabenv` is an env var management standard created by [Carlo Taleon](http://carlo.tl) to minimize env var schema + documentation drift in any codebase. If you follow this standard, you'll find it extremely seamless to "develop locally" and "deploy to production" in any platform!

## Why use it

- Typesafety & Validation
- Good documentation. Never stale, does what it says.
-  Seamless *local development*to*deployment*story.
- No new config files. Your team doesn't need to install crabenv, it's just manual-crud made automated via CLI.
- Language-agnostic. No need to learn language-specific configurations for multi-language and monorepos, just use the same CLI commands.

## Installation

` | `## Quickstart

💡 Before anything else, read this 1-page concept of the standard

[here](https://crabenv.pages.dev/#concepts). Must knowLocal (,`.env`)Schema (,`env.ts`, etc.)Template (`.env.example`)

- This command auto-detects your project and creates a Local, Schema, and Template

```
```
- Add an env var

```
# Notice that Local, Template, and Schema are correctly synced 🎉
```
- List your env vars to see if it's used, remove, or update vars

```
```
😎 That's it! Now imagine the convenience when...

- A new dev onboards on a new project, they just need to do `crabenv cp`to get a correct`.env`file! It's a better`cp .env.example .env`command!
- A senior dev wants to deploy a monorepo so what env vars needed for specific apps? Show them all with `crabenv ls`
- A senior dev wants to reorganize, sort, standardize the structure of env vars? Re-sort them without thinking about it with `crabenv fmt`
- A senior dev wants to check for any drift? `crabenv doctor`

## 📁 Languages supported

Regardless of the language or mix of languages in your repositories, you'll be able to use the same commands.

- 💙 TypeScript/Javascript and Monorepos (includes React, Solid, Vue, Svelte, Vite, NextJS, ReactNative, Backends, and Cloudflare apps)
- 🐍 Python
- 🦀 Rust
- 🐦 Flutter
- More? Request an adapter via issue (the conventional standard must be discussed).

## Agent skill

Completely optional, but in case you want your agent to be autonomous when adding new env vars... Install the crabenv skill for coding agents with:

```
```

# shikumi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/shikumi/0.1.122/shikumi/

## Expand description

Shikumi (仕組み) — config discovery, hot-reload, and `ArcSwap` store
for Nix-managed desktop applications.

Extracted from [karakuri](https://github.com/pleme-io/karakuri)’s configuration
system, shikumi provides the shared infrastructure for desktop apps that need:

- **XDG config discovery**with env var overrides and format preference
- **Figment provider chains**(defaults → env vars → config file)
- **Lock-free concurrent reads**via- `ArcSwap`
- **Hot-reload**with symlink-aware file watching (for nix-darwin managed configs)

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use serde::Deserialize;
use shikumi::{ConfigDiscovery, ConfigStore, Format};
#[derive(Deserialize, Clone, Debug, Default)]
struct MyConfig {
    window_width: Option<u32>,
}
let path = ConfigDiscovery::new("myapp")
    .env_override("MYAPP_CONFIG")
    .formats(&[Format::Yaml, Format::Toml])
    .discover()
    .expect("config file not found");
let store = ConfigStore::<MyConfig>::load(&path, "MYAPP_")
    .expect("failed to load config");
let config = store.get();
println!("width: {:?}", config.window_width);
```

- Emit the canonical `(Display, FromStr, Serialize, Deserialize)`string-surface quartet for a`crate::ClosedAxisLabel`
- [closed_](https://docs.rs/macro.closed_axis_label_string_surface_typed_err.html)- axis_ - label_ - string_ - surface_ - typed_ - err
- Emit the canonical
`(Display, FromStr, Serialize, Deserialize)`string-surface quartet for a closed-axis-label primitive whose`FromStr::Err`is a bespoke typed label-carrying error struct — the sibling lift of`closed_axis_label_string_surface!``crate::ModalityClass``crate::SupportCardinalityClass``crate::SupportBoundaryDistance``crate::SupportMagnitudeDirection``crate::PartitionFace``Result<_, _>`shape rather than the`crate::ShikumiError::Parse``closed_axis_label_string_surface!`
- [perm_](https://docs.rs/macro.perm_cube.html)- cube
- Mechanically emit a `crate::ProductCube``crate::ClosedAxis``const ALL`(full Cartesian product) +`impl ClosedAxis`+`impl ProductCube`.
- [serde_](https://docs.rs/macro.serde_via_display_fromstr.html)- via_ - display_ - fromstr
- Emit the canonical `(Serialize, Deserialize)`serde pair for any type whose canonical scalar form is its`std::fmt::Display``std::str::FromStr`
- [tiered_](https://docs.rs/macro.tiered_permutation_test.html)- permutation_ - test
- Emit ONE matrix `#[test]`that stamps every cube cell onto every config tier, serde-round-trips each, runs a user`apply`closure, and aggregates EVERY failure before asserting.

- [Shikumi](https://docs.rs/enum.ShikumiErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind
- Closed partition over the `ShikumiError`
- [Support](https://docs.rs/enum.SupportBoundaryDistance.html)- Boundary - Distance
- Typed three-bucket projection of the support-cardinality scalar by
**distance from the support-cardinality boundary**— the closed enum lift of the (`is_boundary`,`is_singular`,`is_strict_partial_cover`) strict ternary partition on`SupportCardinalityClass``match`site on the ternary.
- [Support](https://docs.rs/enum.SupportCardinalityClass.html)- Cardinality - Class
- The **support-cardinality classification**of an`AxisHistogram``(observed, unobserved)`cell-partition surface — the five-corner exhaustive partition of the support-cardinality interval`[0, axis_cardinality::<A>()]`.
- [Support](https://docs.rs/enum.SupportMagnitudeDirection.html)- Magnitude - Direction
- Typed three-bucket projection of the support-cardinality scalar by
**support-magnitude direction**— the closed enum lift of the (`is_low_support`,`is_strict_partial_cover`,`is_high_support`) strict ternary partition on`SupportCardinalityClass``SupportBoundaryDistance``SupportCardinalityClass::StrictPartialCover`
- [Watch](https://docs.rs/enum.WatchEventClass.html)- Event - Class
- Reload-relevance class of a file-watch `notify::Event`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Closed](https://docs.rs/trait.ClosedAxis.html)- Axis
- Closed discipline trait every typescape closed-axis primitive and every typescape product cube satisfies.
- [Closed](https://docs.rs/trait.ClosedAxisLabel.html)- Axis - Label
- Closed labeling discipline trait — adds the canonical operator-facing
string label on top of `ClosedAxis`
- [Config](https://docs.rs/trait.ConfigSourceChain.html)- Source - Chain
- Chain-level provenance queries over a recorded `ConfigSource`
- [Partial](https://docs.rs/trait.PartialInverseCube.html)- Inverse - Cube
- Closed discipline trait for the `ProductCube``invert(cell) = Some(image)`exactly on the realizable cells,`None`on the cross-axis consistency-violation complement.
- [Product](https://docs.rs/trait.ProductCube.html)- Cube
- Closed discipline trait every typescape product cube satisfies — a
refinement of `ClosedAxis`

# kigumi_storage - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kigumi-storage/0.1.0/kigumi_storage/

## Expand description

Content-addressed blob storage. Binary attachments live behind an interchangeable [ BlobStore](https://docs.rs/trait.BlobStore.html),
keyed by the sha256 of their content: identical bytes dedupe to one immutable object, and every

`put` re-verifies the hash so the content-address invariant is enforced, never trusted.v1 ships [ FsBlobStore](https://docs.rs/struct.FsBlobStore.html) (files at

`<root>/ab/cd/<hash>`). The API is buffered (a whole blob is held
in memory); streaming for very large blobs (the backup/restore path) is a later enhancement —
attachments are single files of modest size. `S3BlobStore` / `DbBlobStore` are out of v1.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [FsBlob](https://docs.rs/struct.FsBlobStore.html)- Store
- Filesystem blob store: immutable, deduplicated files at `<root>/ab/cd/<hash>`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Blob](https://docs.rs/enum.BlobError.html)- Error
- Errors a blob store can return.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Blob](https://docs.rs/trait.BlobStore.html)- Store
- An interchangeable, content-addressed binary store.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [sha256_](https://docs.rs/fn.sha256_hex.html)- hex
- The sha256 of `bytes`as lowercase hex — the content address used as a blob key.

---

# kigumi_config - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kigumi-config/0.1.0/kigumi_config/

## Expand description

Typed instance configuration — the principled replacement for `odoo.conf`.

Two planes (see `docs/OPERATIONS.md`):

- **boot-time**(this crate): non-secret settings from- `defaults < kigumi.toml < env`, parsed into a typed- `Config`- **fail-fast**(a typo in a core section refuses to boot, unlike- `odoo.conf`which silently ignores it).
- **secrets**: never in the file —- `Secrets`

Connection identity is the single `DATABASE_URL` (a complete DSN); `[database]` carries only
non-URL tuning, so there is no ambiguous overlap. Runtime settings (base_url, mode, neutralized,
banner) are NOT here — they live in the database and are authoritative there.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Auth](https://docs.rs/struct.Auth.html)
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.Config.html)
- Boot-time configuration (everything serializable to `kigumi.toml`; never a secret).
- [Database](https://docs.rs/struct.Database.html)
- Connection TUNING only — the connection identity (host/port/db/user/password/sslmode) is the
single `DATABASE_URL`env var, so there is no host/name field here to conflict with it.
- [Instance](https://docs.rs/struct.Instance.html)
- [Log](https://docs.rs/struct.Log.html)
- [Mail](https://docs.rs/struct.Mail.html)
- [Modules](https://docs.rs/struct.Modules.html)
- Core `[modules]`keys are strict, but each`[modules.<name>]`subtree is OPEN — captured verbatim and validated by the owning module at load, so a module can carry its own settings without the instance refusing to boot.
- [Secrets](https://docs.rs/struct.Secrets.html)
- All runtime secrets. Construct via `Secrets::from_env`
- [Server](https://docs.rs/struct.Server.html)
- [Settings](https://docs.rs/struct.Settings.html)
- The full effective settings: boot-time `Config``Secrets`
- [Storage](https://docs.rs/struct.Storage.html)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [redact_](https://docs.rs/fn.redact_db_url.html)- db_ - url
- Masks the password component of a DSN while keeping host/port/db/user visible — safe to print.

# turbo_surf_mcp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/turbo-surf-mcp/0.3.3/turbo_surf_mcp/

## Expand description

turbo-surf MCP server core (port of `mcp/`) — a stateful agent session over
a current page `Tree`, exposed via stdio JSON-RPC 2.0. No Node, no SDK: the
JSON-RPC envelope is hand-rolled (`initialize` / `tools/list` / `tools/call`).

`goto` fetches + parses into the session; the read tools (markdown / text /
html / links / interactive_elements / accessibility_tree / aria_snapshot /
extract / hydration_state / query / get_by / detect) run over that `Tree`.
Action tools (click/fill/submit) need the navigation state machine and land
with the tier-2 `Page` wiring.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Session](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html)
- One agent session: the current page URL + parsed tree + nav history, plus the browser-ish state agents expect (UA / extra headers / cookie jar / JS mode) and the trails the JS server exposes (rendered-DOM history + a request log).

---

# kigumi_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kigumi-macros/0.1.0/kigumi_macros/

## Expand description

Framework macros. Phase 2: `#[model]` generates the static `ModelDescriptor` + `impl Model`
from an annotated struct, eliminating hand-written descriptors.

The input struct is a declarative DSL: its field “types” (`Text`, `Many2one`, …)
are keywords that the macro maps onto `FieldKind`; the original struct is REPLACED
by a marker type (`pub struct SaleOrder;`) on which the user can write methods.

The generated code uses absolute paths `::kigumi::prelude::…`, so modules must
depend on the `kigumi` facade crate (this is already the workspace convention).

---

# diffler_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/diffler-core/0.2.7/diffler_core/

## Expand description

Core review engine for diffler: diff computation, sessions, comments, viewed marks.

This crate holds all logic with no terminal dependency, so it can be tested headless and reused by the TUI, the MCP server, and future frontends.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [diff](https://docs.rs/diff/index.html)
- Intra-line diff: byte ranges of changed regions between a paired old/new line, used for char-level emphasis on top of line diffs.
- [feedback](https://docs.rs/feedback/index.html)
- Markdown export of review feedback: comments with diff context, ready to paste into any agent prompt.
- [git](https://docs.rs/git/index.html)
- git2 backend for the `Vcs`
- [highlight](https://docs.rs/highlight/index.html)
- Whole-file syntax highlighting via tree-sitter, sliced into per-line styled ranges. Highlighting whole files (not hunks) keeps multi-line constructs like strings correct across hunk boundaries. Unknown languages and parse failures degrade to plain (empty) ranges so rendering never breaks.
- [model](https://docs.rs/model/index.html)
- Diff model: what changed, organized as files -> hunks -> lines.
- [pairing](https://docs.rs/pairing/index.html)
- Pair deleted/added line runs inside a hunk and attach intra-line emphasis. Lines pair positionally within a run, gated by similarity, mirroring delta’s homologous-line model.
- [repo](https://docs.rs/repo/index.html)
- Repository discovery.
- [review](https://docs.rs/review/index.html)
- Facade tying the VCS backend, session, and store together: the one entry point the TUI and MCP layers consume.
- [session](https://docs.rs/session/index.html)
- Review session: comments and per-file viewed marks, reconciled against
fresh diff models. Persistence lives in `store`.
- [source](https://docs.rs/source/index.html)
- What a review is *of*: the working tree, a single commit, or a contiguous commit range. A source has a deterministic, filesystem-safe persistence key and a human-facing label, so review state can be tracked per source and the agent can be told exactly what the human reviewed.
- [store](https://docs.rs/store/index.html)
- Session persistence: one file per review source under `.diffler/reviews/`, atomically written, self-gitignored. The legacy single-session file`.diffler/session.json`is read once and migrated to`reviews/working.json`.
- [syntax](https://docs.rs/syntax/index.html)
- Tree-sitter foundation shared by highlighting, scope context, and the
structural diff. Grammars are statically linked (no runtime loading, since
musl-static binaries cannot `dlopen`); a parse failure or unknown language degrades silently to plain behavior so the UI is never blocked.
- [vcs](https://docs.rs/vcs/index.html)
- Backend-agnostic VCS interface. Everything above this trait consumes
`dyn Vcs`; only the`git`module (and test fixtures) may import git2.

---

# kigumi_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kigumi-core/0.1.0/kigumi_core/

## Expand description

Kigumi core: the inspectable metamodel + the module versioning model.

Difference from Odoo (see `docs/ANALISI_ODOO19.md`): a model definition is NOT
a class synthesized at runtime with `type()`, but inspectable static data;
extension is a VERIFIED MERGE, not a global monkey-patch; dependencies between
modules have verified VERSION RANGES (Odoo does not have them — see `docs/VERSIONING.md`).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [inventory](https://docs.rs/inventory/0.3.24/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/inventory/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Acl](https://docs.rs/struct.Acl.html)
- Model-level access grant for one group (the `ir.model.access`analog).
- [AclRegistration](https://docs.rs/struct.AclRegistration.html)
- Registration of a module’s ACLs (emitted by `register_acls!`). Compile-time security data; M6 adds a DB-backed loader on top, but the in-code registry stays the bootstrap/default source.
- [Action](https://docs.rs/struct.ActionInput.html)- Input
- Read-only view of the record an action runs on (its current stored values), with typed accessors.
- [Action](https://docs.rs/struct.ActionOutcome.html)- Outcome
- What an action produces: field updates to apply, plus an optional “assign field = next_value(code)” directive resolved by the persistence layer (which can call the sequence engine).
- [Action](https://docs.rs/struct.ActionRegistration.html)- Registration
- Registration of an action by (model, name), emitted by `register_action!`.`groups`(if non-empty) restricts who may run it, on top of the model’s Write ACL + record rules.
- [Compute](https://docs.rs/struct.ComputeInput.html)- Input
- Read-only view of a record (its own fields + its One2many children), passed to a compute
function. Same-record computes read `int`/`float`/…; aggregate computes read`children`/`sum_float`.
- [Compute](https://docs.rs/struct.ComputeRegistration.html)- Registration
- Registration of a compute function by name (emitted by `register_compute!`).
- [Condition](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html)
- A single leaf condition `field <op> value`.
- [Constraint](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstraintRegistration.html)- Registration
- Registration of a constraint on a model, evaluated when any of `fields`is written (an empty`fields`runs on every write). Emitted by`register_constraint!`.
- [Constraint](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstraintViolation.html)- Violation
- A constraint violation: the failing rule’s message plus the fields the rule DECLARED as its triggers — the fields a form should highlight. Empty for an unconditional (whole-record) rule.
- [Ctx](https://docs.rs/struct.Ctx.html)
- Evaluation context: who is acting, and whether checks are bypassed.
- [Delegated](https://docs.rs/struct.DelegatedField.html)- Field
- A field a child transparently exposes from its `_inherits`parent: the parent’s`FieldDef``via`FK column the read subquery / write UPDATE pivots on.
- [External](https://docs.rs/struct.ExternalTable.html)- Table
- A model whose table is owned OUTSIDE the metamodel (e.g. the auth subsystem’s `kigumi_user`, or a SQL view): registered so it is resolved/served like any model, but EXCLUDED from migration — the metamodel never creates or alters its table. Odoo’s`_auto = False`. Emitted by`register_external!`.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldBuilder.html)- Builder
- Fluent builder for a single condition.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldDef.html)- Def
- Definition of a single field.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldExtension.html)- Extension
- Registration of a field extension (emitted by `#[extend]`).
- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldGroup.html)- Group
- A titled group of scalar fields, laid out in two columns. `title`is optional (a lead group with no heading is common for the identity fields).
- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldGroupRegistration.html)- Group - Registration
- Field-level access restriction (D6 / Odoo’s `Field.groups`): the groups required to access one`model.field`. Registered out-of-band (emitted by`#[field(groups = "...")]`) so it adds no column to the metamodel and no churn to existing`FieldDef`literals — the same side-registry pattern as external tables. Read AND write are gated by the same set, at the DB boundary.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldSlot.html)- Slot
- A field placed in a group. `full`makes it span both columns — use it for relations, long text (Html), images, and the primary name.
- [Form](https://docs.rs/struct.FormView.html)- View
- A model’s form layout. Emitted by `register_view!`.
- [Inherits](https://docs.rs/struct.InheritsRegistration.html)- Registration
- Delegation inheritance (Odoo’s `_inherits`):`model`carries a required Many2one`via`to`parent`and transparently exposes the parent’s stored scalar fields (read via the FK, written through to the parent). Emitted by`#[model(inherits = "parent", via = "fk")]`. The`via`FK is an ordinary field the model declares — this only records the delegation, so no`ModelDescriptor`/`FieldDef`churn.
- [Mailed](https://docs.rs/struct.MailedRegistration.html)- Registration
- A model that opts INTO the mail subsystem (chatter): it gains a thread of `mail.message`s, followers and activities, addressed by the polymorphic`(res_model, res_id)`link. Emitted by`register_mailed!`. Unlike Odoo’s 5118-line`mail.thread`mixin, this is a one-line compile-time marker the framework iterates — to gate the chatter API and to clean up the thread on delete.
- [Migration](https://docs.rs/struct.MigrationTarget.html)- Target
- One model to migrate, with the owning module’s name + version (for the migration ledger).
- [Model](https://docs.rs/struct.ModelDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Descriptor of a model as defined by ONE module (the “base”).
- [Model](https://docs.rs/struct.ModelRegistration.html)- Registration
- Registration of a base model (emitted by `#[model]`).
- [Module](https://docs.rs/struct.ModuleDep.html)- Dep
- Dependency on another module, with a SemVer version constraint (e.g. “^1.2”).
- [Module](https://docs.rs/struct.ModuleManifest.html)- Manifest
- Manifest of a module. Declarative data, validated at build/install time.
- [Module](https://docs.rs/struct.ModuleRegistration.html)- Registration
- Registration of a module manifest (emitted by `register_module!`).`crate_path`is the Rust module path of the registering crate (`module_path!()`), used to map a model — whose own registration carries`module_path!()`— back to its owning manifest (name + version).
- [Notebook](https://docs.rs/struct.NotebookPage.html)- Page
- A notebook page (tab) below the sheet, usually a One2many relation or grouped secondary fields.
- [Readonly](https://docs.rs/struct.ReadonlyFieldRegistration.html)- Field - Registration
- A stored field declared read-only: shown in the UI contract as `readonly`and rejected by the write path (like a computed field), even though it is not computed. Emitted by`#[field(readonly)]`. Used for materialized values a service method maintains (e.g. on-hand) — visible, never hand-edited.
- [Record](https://docs.rs/struct.RecordRule.html)- Rule
- Row-level rule (the `ir.rule`analog).`groups`empty = global (applies to everyone).
- [Record](https://docs.rs/struct.RecordRuleRegistration.html)- Rule - Registration
- Registration of a module’s record rules (emitted by `register_rules!`).
- [Related](https://docs.rs/struct.RelatedRegistration.html)- Registration
- A related field (Odoo `related=`): a NON-stored, read-only mirror of a value reached by following a relational`path`(e.g.`order_id.currency_id`). Registered out-of-band (emitted by`#[field(related = "...")]`) so it adds no column to the metamodel — the value is resolved at read time by a correlated subquery over the path. The field’s declared kind must match the path target.
- [Report](https://docs.rs/struct.ReportRegistration.html)- Registration
- Registration of a report by (model, name), emitted by `register_report!`.`name`is the URL segment (e.g. “quotation”);`title`is the human label used in the contract and the download filename.
- [Resolved](https://docs.rs/struct.ResolvedModel.html)- Model
- RESOLVED descriptor: base + all extensions merged and validated. This is the point — absent in Odoo — where the final definition is materializable.
- [Sequence](https://docs.rs/struct.SequenceRegistration.html)- Registration
- A module’s document-numbering sequence (emitted by `register_sequence!`): declared next to the action that consumes it, ensured at migrate — an existing sequence keeps its counter.`module`is diagnostic only (a cross-module code collision is reported with both names).
- [Sql](https://docs.rs/struct.Sql.html)
- Compiled SQL: a boolean expression plus its ordered bound parameters.
- [Tracked](https://docs.rs/struct.TrackedFieldRegistration.html)- Field - Registration
- A field whose changes are tracked in the chatter (Odoo’s `tracking=True`). When a write changes it on a mailed model, the write path records a`notification`message + a typed`mail.tracking`row (old → new). Emitted by`#[field(tracked)]`. Compile-time, not runtime`track_visibility`.
- [Transient](https://docs.rs/struct.TransientRegistration.html)- Registration
- A model whose rows are ephemeral (Odoo’s `TransientModel`): a wizard scratchpad with its own table, served and secured like any model, but periodically garbage-collected by age. Emitted by`register_transient!`. A transient model declares a nullable`create_date Datetime`; migration gives that column a`DEFAULT now()`so every insert is timestamped and the GC cron can reclaim it.
- [Wizard](https://docs.rs/struct.WizardContext.html)- Context
- The records a wizard is opened against (Odoo’s `active_model`/`active_id`/`active_ids`context).
- [Wizard](https://docs.rs/struct.WizardRegistration.html)- Registration
- Registration of a wizard (emitted by `register_wizard!`): binds a transient model to its`default_get`. The model must also be`register_transient!`-marked (so its rows are GC’d).

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Domain](https://docs.rs/enum.Domain.html)
- A filter expression. Combine with `and`/`or`/`not`.
- [Domain](https://docs.rs/enum.DomainError.html)- Error
- [Field](https://docs.rs/enum.FieldKind.html)- Kind
- Logical type of a field. From this we derive the SQL type, UI widget, and API type.
- [Operation](https://docs.rs/enum.Operation.html)
- A CRUD operation subject to access control.
- [Operator](https://docs.rs/enum.Operator.html)
- [Resolution](https://docs.rs/enum.ResolutionError.html)- Error
- [Rule](https://docs.rs/enum.RuleDomain.html)- Domain
- The domain source of a `RecordRule``Static`(a thunk, because a`Domain``Owned`, holding a domain parsed at load time. The engine treats both identically — only where the domain comes from differs, so static and DB rules merge into one list with no special-casing.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html)
- A scalar (or list) literal used on the right-hand side of a condition.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [FRAMEWORK_](https://docs.rs/constant.FRAMEWORK_VERSION.html)- VERSION
- Framework SemVer version (= workspace version). Modules compare it
against their own compatibility range via `check_compat`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Model](https://docs.rs/trait.Model.html)
- Implemented by every model. In the walking skeleton it is written by hand;
in phase 2 it is generated by the `#[model]`proc-macro.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [action_](https://docs.rs/fn.action_for.html)- for
- Looks up a registered action by model + name.
- [actions_](https://docs.rs/fn.actions_for.html)- for
- All actions registered on `model`(for the UI contract, so a form can render its action buttons).
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_access.html)- access
- Returns true if `ctx`may perform`op`on`model`. Access is granted if ANY of the user’s groups grants it (union semantics, like Odoo). Superuser is always allowed.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_compat.html)- compat
- Verifies that `manifest`is compatible with the provided framework version. This is the check Odoo does NOT do: there a “19.0” module runs (or breaks) on any 19.x.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_constraints.html)- constraints
- Runs the model’s constraints over a just-written record (`values`+ its`children`).`changed`is the set of written field names, or`None`on create (every constraint runs). A constraint runs when it is unconditional (empty`fields`), on create, or when one of its trigger`fields`was written. Returns the first violation (message + the rule’s declared fields), which the caller maps to a typed error that rolls back the tx.
- [compute_](https://docs.rs/fn.compute_fn.html)- fn
- Looks up a registered compute function by its declared name.
- [compute_](https://docs.rs/fn.compute_on_read.html)- on_ - read
- Evaluates the model’s NON-stored computed fields (Odoo `compute=`without`store=True`) over a record’s`values`at READ time, returning the (name, value) pairs to inject into the projection. These have no column and are never written — they are derived on every read. Same-record:`children`is empty, so a function reads the record’s own scalar fields plus any related / delegated values already present in`values`(both are read alongside the columns), not its One2many children.
- [compute_](https://docs.rs/fn.compute_stored.html)- stored
- Fills `values`with the result of each stored computed field whose function is registered, given the record’s own fields and its One2many`children`(for aggregate computes). Computes from a snapshot taken BEFORE writing any result, so computes read the inputs (chained compute-on-compute is not ordered — out of scope).
- [computed_](https://docs.rs/fn.computed_fields.html)- fields
- Names of the model’s stored computed fields that have a registered function.
- [delegated_](https://docs.rs/fn.delegated_fields.html)- fields
- The fields `model`delegates to its`_inherits`parent (empty if it is not a child). Each is read via the parent through the`via`FK; the child does NOT have a column for it. A name the child also declares (an intentional shadow, e.g.`product.product.active`over`product.template.active`) is excluded — the child’s own column wins and the parent’s is not delegated.
- [external_](https://docs.rs/fn.external_tables.html)- tables
- Names of models whose tables the metamodel must NOT migrate (owned externally).
- [field_](https://docs.rs/fn.field_accessible.html)- accessible
- Whether `ctx`may access (read or write)`model.field`. Default-allow when the field has no group restriction; superuser always allowed; otherwise the caller must be in at least one required group. Mirrors Odoo, which gates read and write by the same`Field.groups`set at the ORM boundary.
- [field_](https://docs.rs/fn.field_is_readonly.html)- is_ - readonly
- Whether `model`.`field`is declared`#[field(readonly)]`.
- [field_](https://docs.rs/fn.field_required_groups.html)- required_ - groups
- The groups required to access `model.field`, or None when the field is unrestricted. Delegation- aware (`_inherits`): a restriction on an inherited field lives on the PARENT model, so when the field is not restricted directly on`model`we fall back to the parent — otherwise an inherited field would expose its restricted value through the child (read/order/filter). Recurses the chain. Shadow-aware: a name the child declares as its OWN column (e.g.`product.product.active`over`product.template.active`) does NOT borrow the parent’s restriction — only genuinely delegated fields fall back, so a group added to the parent never silently gates the child’s own column.
- [has_](https://docs.rs/fn.has_constraints.html)- constraints
- True iff the model has any registered constraint — a cheap gate before the in-transaction re-read
that `check_constraints`
- [has_](https://docs.rs/fn.has_read_computes.html)- read_ - computes
- True iff the model has any NON-stored computed field (a cheap gate before doing the extra decode
that `compute_on_read`
- [inherits_](https://docs.rs/fn.inherits_of.html)- of
- The `(parent, via)`a model delegates to, or None if it is not an`_inherits`child.
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_mailed.html)- mailed
- Whether `model`has a mail thread (chatter enabled).
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_transient.html)- transient
- Whether `model`is transient (its rows are garbage-collected by age).
- [json_](https://docs.rs/fn.json_string.html)- string
- JSON-escapes `s`and wraps it in double quotes. Shared by domain and UI-contract serialization so every string in the emitted JSON is escaped consistently (no broken-out quotes).
- [mailed_](https://docs.rs/fn.mailed_models.html)- models
- Names of all models that opted into the mail subsystem.
- [migration_](https://docs.rs/fn.migration_plan.html)- plan
- The full migration plan, TOPOLOGICALLY SORTED by Many2one FK dependencies (a model’s FK targets — e.g. res.currency/res.partner for res.company — are created before the referencing table). Self-references are ignored (a table may reference itself in its own CREATE); a genuine FK cycle between two tables is an error. Ties break by (module dependency order, model name) for determinism. Each target carries its owning module’s name + version for the migration ledger.
- [module_](https://docs.rs/fn.module_closure.html)- closure
- A module plus its full transitive dependency closure, in dependency order (dependencies first) —
the set to install when installing `name`. Errors if`name`(or a dependency) is not a linked module, or the module graph is invalid.
- [module_](https://docs.rs/fn.module_of.html)- of
- The name of the module that owns `model`, via the model’s registration crate_path → manifest mapping (the same hook`migration_plan`uses). Used to gate migration/serving by installed module.
- [record_](https://docs.rs/fn.record_rule_domain.html)- rule_ - domain
- Combines the record rules applicable to (`op`,`model`,`ctx`) into a single restricting`Domain``None`when nothing restricts (superuser, or no applicable rule).
- [registered_](https://docs.rs/fn.registered_acls.html)- acls
- All ACLs registered across linked modules (the union a server enforces).
- [registered_](https://docs.rs/fn.registered_group_names.html)- group_ - names
- Distinct group names referenced by any registered ACL or record rule — the catalog’s known
groups (the source for seeding the read-only `res.groups`list). Sorted, deterministic.
- [registered_](https://docs.rs/fn.registered_model_names.html)- model_ - names
- Names of all models registered in the catalog (sorted, deterministic).
- [registered_](https://docs.rs/fn.registered_rules.html)- rules
- All record rules registered across linked modules.
- [registered_](https://docs.rs/fn.registered_sequences.html)- sequences
- All sequences registered across linked modules.
- [related_](https://docs.rs/fn.related_path.html)- path
- The relational path a related field mirrors, or None if `field`is not a related field.
- [report_](https://docs.rs/fn.report_for.html)- for
- Looks up a registered report by model + name.
- [reports_](https://docs.rs/fn.reports_for.html)- for
- All reports registered on `model`(for the UI contract, so a form can offer its “Print” buttons).
- [resolve](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve.html)
- Merges the base with the module extensions. Conflicts are errors.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_all_registered.html)- all_ - registered
- Resolves every registered model (base + extensions). The bridge from the catalog to a server or any consumer that needs the full set of models.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_module_set.html)- module_ - set
- Resolves a set of modules: checks framework compatibility, that every dependency exists with a satisfying SemVer version, that there are no duplicate names and no cycles. Returns the modules in dependency (topological) order — what Odoo computes implicitly.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_modules.html)- modules
- Resolves every module registered in the catalog: framework compatibility, dependency
version ranges, no duplicates, no cycles — returning them in dependency order.
The validation `resolve_module_set`does is exactly what Odoo’s`depends`cannot express.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_registered.html)- registered
- Resolves a model from the CATALOG: registered base + all auto-registered extensions, merged (with conflict checks) and validated. No wiring: modules auto-register.
- [tracked_](https://docs.rs/fn.tracked_fields.html)- fields
- The names of `model`’s tracked fields (changes recorded in the chatter on write).
- [transient_](https://docs.rs/fn.transient_models.html)- models
- Names of all transient (ephemeral / wizard) models.
- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_depends.html)- depends
- Verifies that each `depends`points to an existing field (first segment of the path). Antidote to Odoo’s silent N+1: a broken dependency is an error, not a runtime bug.
- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_depends_with_extra.html)- depends_ - with_ - extra
- Like `validate_depends``extra`lists additional valid first-segment names — the`_inherits`delegated fields, which have no column on`m`yet are readable on the record (so an on-read compute may depend on, e.g., the inherited`name`). The registry passes the delegated names here.
- [view_](https://docs.rs/fn.view_for.html)- for
- The registered form view for `model`, if any (else the frontend applies a smart default layout).
- [wizard_](https://docs.rs/fn.wizard_for.html)- for
- Looks up a registered wizard by model name.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Action](https://docs.rs/type.ActionFn.html)- Fn
- A registered action: a pure transition function. Guards (e.g. “only a draft”) live in the body
and return `Err(message)`to refuse the transition.
- [Children](https://docs.rs/type.Children.html)
- One2many children grouped by the o2m field name (each child is its own field→value map).
- [Compute](https://docs.rs/type.ComputeFn.html)- Fn
- A registered compute function.
- [Constraint](https://docs.rs/type.ConstraintFn.html)- Fn
- A constraint over a just-written record: returns `Err(message)`to reject (and roll back) the write.
- [Report](https://docs.rs/type.ReportFn.html)- Fn
- Renders a record — with its inlined One2many children, exactly as `find_one_secured`returns it — to a complete HTML document. Pure: no DB access and no recompute; it reads only the fields present.
- [Wizard](https://docs.rs/type.WizardDefaultGet.html)- Default - Get
- Computes a wizard’s seed field values from the context (Odoo’s `default_get`). Pure in v1 (no DB reads); DB-backed defaults are a later extension done by a dedicated open service method.

# openipc_video - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/openipc-video/0.1.27/openipc_video/

## Expand description

Low-latency platform video decoding for OpenIPC applications.

The crate accepts complete Annex-B access units, keeps codec parsing and backpressure behavior platform-neutral, and delegates actual decoding to a platform decoder. H.264 and H.265 are supported by the shared API.

# rocq2md - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rocq2md/0.1.0/rocq2md/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rocq2md)rocq2md

A library for converting Rocq files to Markdown.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- Converts top-level `(* ... *)`comments (starting at column 0, outside of any`Proof ... Qed`/`Defined`/`Admitted`/`Abort`environment) into plain Markdown text.
- Leaves all other Rocq source (including comments that were not
converted) inside ````rocq`code fences.
- Warns about comment blocks that were not converted because they did not start at the beginning of a line (comments inside proofs are silently left as-is).
- Supports a `--#-- ... --#--`marker pair to strip text out of a converted comment block, usable inline or across multiple lines.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Conversion](https://docs.rs/struct.ConversionReport.html)- Report
- The result of parsing/converting a single piece of Rocq source: any
warnings encountered, plus the number of `--#-- ... --#--`blocks that were stripped from the output (informational only, not a warning).

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Segment](https://docs.rs/enum.Segment.html)
- A piece of the output: either plain Markdown text (extracted from a converted comment block) or a chunk of raw Rocq source that should be rendered inside a ```rocq code fence.
- [Warning](https://docs.rs/enum.Warning.html)
- A single anomaly found while parsing a Rocq source file.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_segments.html)- segments
- Parses Rocq source text into a sequence of Markdown/Code segments.
- [convert_](https://docs.rs/fn.convert_to_markdown.html)- to_ - markdown
- Converts Rocq source text into a Markdown document.
- [process_](https://docs.rs/fn.process_directory.html)- directory
- Processes a directory of Rocq files and converts them to Markdown.
- [process_](https://docs.rs/fn.process_file.html)- file
- Processes a single Rocq file and converts it to Markdown.

# turbo_surf_raster - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/turbo-surf-raster/0.3.3/turbo_surf_raster/

## Expand description

Synthetic screenshots for turbo-surf: turn an HTML **snapshot** into a PNG or
SVG image with no browser and no rendering surface of our own.

The engine borrows turbo-html2pdf’s native HTML/CSS **layout** (block/inline/
flex/table + real font shaping over bundled faces) to turn a raw HTML string
into a positioned [ Fragment](https://docs.rs/turbo-html2pdf-core/0.2.6/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/turbo_html2pdf_core/layout/fragment/struct.Fragment.html) display list, then paints that list two ways:
a raster [

`paint_png`] (tiny-skia) and a vector [`paint_svg`]. Both walk the
same fragments in CSS stacking (paint) order via `Fragment::paint_order`, so
they agree.This is a *reasonably representative* render, not a pixel-faithful browser:
`position`/`z-index` are honored for block flow (out-of-flow boxes are placed
against their containing block and painted back-to-front per CSS 2.2 §9.9),
and `<img>`/`background-image` bytes the caller supplies are decoded + painted
(PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP + SVG; unknown formats fall back to a placeholder) — but
there is no JS-driven visual state beyond whatever produced the snapshot. It
runs only when asked — never on the fetch/extract hot path.

Because the input is just an HTML string, any snapshot works: the initial fetch, or any entry in a hydration trail.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Viewport](https://docs.rs/struct.Viewport.html)
- The layout viewport a snapshot is rendered against. `width`drives CSS layout (line wrapping,`%`widths); the image is`width × height`px and content past the bottom edge is clipped, matching a browser viewport screenshot.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Format](https://docs.rs/enum.Format.html)
- Output encoding for a screenshot.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [delazy_](https://docs.rs/fn.delazy_images.html)- images
- Fill in a missing `<img src>`from its lazy/responsive attribute, so the layout (which sizes/paints an image box from`src`) renders lazy-loaded images whose JS`src`-swap didn’t run headless.`<img>`s that already have a`src`are left as-is. The injected URL matches what`image_urls`
- [image_](https://docs.rs/fn.image_urls.html)- urls
- Every image reference the layout engine can paint, in source order and
de-duplicated: `<img src>`values and`background-image: url(...)`urls. Values are returned**verbatim**— exactly the resolver key turbo-html2pdf uses (the raw`src`, or the unquoted`url(...)`inner) — so the caller resolves each against the page URL, fetches the bytes, and stores them under the same key.`data:`URIs are skipped (self-contained, nothing to fetch).
- [screenshot](https://docs.rs/fn.screenshot.html)
- Dispatch by `Format`
- [screenshot_](https://docs.rs/fn.screenshot_png.html)- png
- Lay `html`out at`viewport`and paint it into a PNG. Returns encoded bytes.
- [screenshot_](https://docs.rs/fn.screenshot_png_with_assets.html)- png_ - with_ - assets
- Like `screenshot_png_with_css``<img>`/`background-image`boxes from caller-fetched`images`(keyed as`image_urls``full_page`, the image height is the full content height (viewport width still drives layout) instead of the viewport height.
- [screenshot_](https://docs.rs/fn.screenshot_png_with_css.html)- png_ - with_ - css
- Like `screenshot_png``external_css`(e.g. the concatenated bodies of the page’s`<link rel="stylesheet">`sheets, fetched by the caller — the raster does no I/O) cascaded on top of the page’s own inline styles.
- [screenshot_](https://docs.rs/fn.screenshot_png_with_opts.html)- png_ - with_ - opts
- `screenshot_png_with_assets`- `system_fonts`: when true, the page’s fonts resolve against the machine’s installed system fonts (matching a browser on the same host) instead of only the bundled fallback faces. Opt-in — it loads the OS font set (cached across calls).
- [screenshot_](https://docs.rs/fn.screenshot_svg.html)- svg
- Lay `html`out at`viewport`and paint it into a standalone SVG document.
- [screenshot_](https://docs.rs/fn.screenshot_svg_with_assets.html)- svg_ - with_ - assets
- Like `screenshot_svg_with_css``images`(see`screenshot_png_with_assets``data:`URIs. With`full_page`, the height is the full content height.
- [screenshot_](https://docs.rs/fn.screenshot_svg_with_css.html)- svg_ - with_ - css
- Like `screenshot_svg``external_css`(see`screenshot_png_with_css`
- [screenshot_](https://docs.rs/fn.screenshot_svg_with_opts.html)- svg_ - with_ - opts
- `screenshot_svg_with_assets`- `system_fonts`(see- `screenshot_png_with_opts`
- [stylesheet_](https://docs.rs/fn.stylesheet_hrefs.html)- hrefs
- The `href`s of every`<link rel="stylesheet">`in`html`, in source order. Values are returned verbatim (possibly relative) — the caller resolves them against the page URL and fetches them (the raster itself does no I/O).`rel`is matched case-insensitively and may carry other tokens (`stylesheet preload`). Alternate stylesheets (`rel="alternate stylesheet"`) are skipped.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Image](https://docs.rs/type.ImageAssets.html)- Assets
- Fetched image bytes keyed by their reference — the raw `<img src>`/`background-image: url(...)`value exactly as`image_urls``*_with_assets`screenshot; both layout (intrinsic sizing) and paint read the same bytes.

# arrayref 0.3.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/arrayref/0.3.9

# arrayref

This is a very small rust module, which contains just four macros, for the taking of array references to slices of... sliceable things. These macros (which are awkwardly named) should be perfectly safe, and have seen just a tad of code review.

## Why would I want this?

The goal of arrayref is to enable the effective use of APIs that
involve array references rather than slices, for situations where
parameters must have a given size.  As an example, consider the
`byteorder` crate.  This is a very nice crate with a simple API
containing functions that look like:

```
;
;
```
Looking at this, you might wonder why they accept a slice reference as input. After all, they always want just two bytes. These functions must panic if given a slice that is too small, which means that unless they are inlined, then a runtime bounds-check is forced, even if it may be statically known that the input is the right size.

Wouldn't it be nicer if we had functions more like

```
;
;
```
The type signature would tell users precisely what size of input is
required, and the compiler could check at compile time that the input
is of the appropriate size: this sounds like the zero-cost
abstractions rust is famous for!  However, there is a catch, which
arises when you try to *use* these nicer functions, which is that
usually you are looking at two bytes in a stream.  So, e.g. consider
that we are working with a hypothetical (and simplified) ipv6 address.

Doing this with our array version (which looks so beautiful in terms of accurately describing what we want!) looks terrible:

```
let addr: & = ...;
let mut segments = ;
// array-based API
for i in 0 .. 8
// slice-based API
for i in 0 .. 8
```
The array-based approach looks way worse.  We need to create a fresh
copy of the bytes, just so it will be in an array of the proper size!
Thus the whole "zero-cost abstraction" argument for using array
references fails.  The trouble is that there is no (safe) way (until
[RFC 495](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/0495-array-pattern-changes.md) lands) to obtain an array reference to a portion of a
larger array or slice.  Doing so is the equivalent of taking a slice
with a size known at compile time, and ought to be built into the
language.

The arrayref crate allows you to do this kind of slicing. So the above (very contrived) example can be implemented with array references as:

```
let addr: & = ...;
let mut segments = ;
// array-based API with arrayref
for i in 0 .. 8
```
Here the `array_ref![addr,2*i,2]` macro allows us to take an array
reference to a slice consisting of two bytes starting at `2*i`.  Apart
from the syntax (less nice than slicing), it is essentially the same
as the slice approach.  However, this code makes explicit the
need for precisely *two* bytes both in the caller, and in the function
signature.

This module provides three other macros providing related
functionality, which you can read about in the
[documentation](https://droundy.github.io/arrayref).

For an example of how these macros can be used in an actual program,
see [my rust translation of tweetnacl](https://github.com/droundy/onionsalt/blob/master/src/crypto/mod.rs), which uses `arrayref`
to almost exclusively accept array references in functions, with the
only exception being those which truly expect data of arbitrary
length.  In my opinion, the result is code that is far more legible
than the original C code, since the size of each argument is
explicit.  Moreover (although I have not tested this), the use of
array references rather than slices *should* result in far fewer
bounds checks, since almost all sizes are known at compile time.

---

# arrayref 0.3.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/arrayref/0.3.9/source/

#
                    arrayref 0.3.9

                Macros to take array references of slices

# arrayref - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/arrayref/0.3.9/target-redirect/arrayref/

## Expand description

This package contains just four macros, which enable the creation of array references to portions of arrays or slices (or things that can be sliced).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Here is a simple example of slicing and dicing a slice into array
references with these macros.  Here we implement a simple
little-endian conversion from bytes to `u16`, and demonstrate code
that uses `array_ref!` to extract an array reference from a larger
array.  Note that the documentation for each macro also has an
example of its use.

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate arrayref;
fn read_u16(bytes: &[u8; 2]) -> u16 {
     bytes[0] as u16 + ((bytes[1] as u16) << 8)
}
// ...
let data = [0,1,2,3,4,0,6,7,8,9];
assert_eq!(256, read_u16(array_ref![data,0,2]));
assert_eq!(4, read_u16(array_ref![data,4,2]));
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [array_](https://docs.rs/macro.array_mut_ref.html)- mut_ - ref
- You can use `array_mut_ref`to generate a mutable array reference to a subset of a sliceable bit of data (which could be an array, or a slice, or a Vec).
- [array_](https://docs.rs/macro.array_ref.html)- ref
- You can use `array_ref`to generate an array reference to a subset of a sliceable bit of data (which could be an array, or a slice, or a Vec).
- [array_](https://docs.rs/macro.array_refs.html)- refs
- You can use `array_refs`to generate a series of array references to an input array reference. The idea is if you want to break an array into a series of contiguous and non-overlapping arrays.`array_refs`is a bit funny in that it insists on slicing up the*entire*array. This is intentional, as I find it handy to make me ensure that my sub-arrays add up to the entire array. This macro will*never*panic, since the sizes are all checked at compile time.
- [mut_](https://docs.rs/macro.mut_array_refs.html)- array_ - refs
- You can use `mut_array_refs`to generate a series of mutable array references to an input mutable array reference. The idea is if you want to break an array into a series of contiguous and non-overlapping mutable array references. Like`array_refs!`,`mut_array_refs!`is a bit funny in that it insists on slicing up the*entire*array. This is intentional, as I find it handy to make me ensure that my sub-arrays add up to the entire array. This macro will*never*panic, since the sizes are all checked at compile time.

# arrayref - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arrayref/0.3.9/arrayref/index.html

## Expand description

This package contains just four macros, which enable the creation of array references to portions of arrays or slices (or things that can be sliced).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Here is a simple example of slicing and dicing a slice into array
references with these macros.  Here we implement a simple
little-endian conversion from bytes to `u16`, and demonstrate code
that uses `array_ref!` to extract an array reference from a larger
array.  Note that the documentation for each macro also has an
example of its use.

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate arrayref;
fn read_u16(bytes: &[u8; 2]) -> u16 {
     bytes[0] as u16 + ((bytes[1] as u16) << 8)
}
// ...
let data = [0,1,2,3,4,0,6,7,8,9];
assert_eq!(256, read_u16(array_ref![data,0,2]));
assert_eq!(4, read_u16(array_ref![data,4,2]));
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [array_](https://docs.rs/macro.array_mut_ref.html)- mut_ - ref
- You can use `array_mut_ref`to generate a mutable array reference to a subset of a sliceable bit of data (which could be an array, or a slice, or a Vec).
- [array_](https://docs.rs/macro.array_ref.html)- ref
- You can use `array_ref`to generate an array reference to a subset of a sliceable bit of data (which could be an array, or a slice, or a Vec).
- [array_](https://docs.rs/macro.array_refs.html)- refs
- You can use `array_refs`to generate a series of array references to an input array reference. The idea is if you want to break an array into a series of contiguous and non-overlapping arrays.`array_refs`is a bit funny in that it insists on slicing up the*entire*array. This is intentional, as I find it handy to make me ensure that my sub-arrays add up to the entire array. This macro will*never*panic, since the sizes are all checked at compile time.
- [mut_](https://docs.rs/macro.mut_array_refs.html)- array_ - refs
- You can use `mut_array_refs`to generate a series of mutable array references to an input mutable array reference. The idea is if you want to break an array into a series of contiguous and non-overlapping mutable array references. Like`array_refs!`,`mut_array_refs!`is a bit funny in that it insists on slicing up the*entire*array. This is intentional, as I find it handy to make me ensure that my sub-arrays add up to the entire array. This macro will*never*panic, since the sizes are all checked at compile time.
